title: Cap. 7 ultimum Patrum: open — Augustine In Joh. tract. 48 on sheep/price
latin: Sed ne nudis nominibus pugnare videamur, ultimum nostrum argumentum petetur ab expressis testimoniis Patrum & modernorum, qui praedestinatis in hac morte Christi specialem praerogativam assignant, quae alia non est quam infallibilis consecutio gratiae & gloriae secundum specialem Dei ordinationem a merito Christi morientis, & pro illis speciali quodam intuitu sese offerentis, derivata. Prodeat primo S. Augustinus. 1. Praeclarum est illud testimonium, In Joh. tract. 48. pag. 352. tom. 9. Quomodo istos dixit, NON ESTIS EX OVIBUS MEIS? Quia videbat eos ad sempiternum interitum praedestinatos, non ad vitam aeternam sui sanguinis pretio comparatos. Paulo post, De ovibus illis nec lupus rapit, nec fur tollit, nec latro interficit. Securus est de numero earum, qui pro eis novit quid dedit. Ex quibus verbis duo colligimus: Unum, Servatorem nostrum pro praedestinatis redimendis pretium sui sanguinis obtulisse speciali quodam modo, eo nimirum ex quo infallibilis salus eorundem consequatur. Alterum, pro praeteritis sive non-praedestinatis haud obtulisse sanguinem suum eo modo: unde negantur ad vitam aeternam sui sanguinis pretio comparati: quod intelligendum est de absoluta & efficaci ordinatione ad vitam aeternam per Christi mortem implenda, & in actum deducenda.
pass_a_gloss: But lest we seem to fight with bare names, let our last argument be drawn from the express testimonies of the Fathers and of the moderns, who assign to the predestined in this death of Christ a special prerogative, which is nothing other than the infallible attainment of grace and glory according to the special ordination of God derived from the merit of the dying Christ, and from him offering himself for them with a certain special regard. Let Saint Augustine come forward first. 1. That testimony is outstanding, In John tractate 48, page 352, volume 9: How did he say of those, YOU ARE NOT OF MY SHEEP? Because he saw them predestined to everlasting ruin, not purchased for eternal life by the price of his blood. A little later: Of those sheep neither wolf snatches, nor thief takes, nor robber kills. He is secure about their number who for them knows what he gave. From which words we gather two things: One, that our Savior offered the price of his blood for redeeming the predestined in a certain special manner, namely that from which their infallible salvation follows. The other, that for the passed-over or non-predestined he did not offer his blood in that manner: whence they are denied to have been purchased for eternal life by the price of his blood — which is to be understood of an absolute and efficacious ordination to eternal life to be fulfilled and brought into act through Christ's death.
pass_b: Lest we seem to argue by empty labels, our last proof comes from the express witnesses of the Fathers and of later writers who give the predestined, in this death of Christ, a special privilege — nothing other than the sure attainment of grace and glory by God's special ordination, drawn from the dying Christ's merit and from his offering himself for them with a particular regard. Let Augustine speak first. 1. Outstanding is the word in In John, tractate 48 (vol. 9, p. 352): How did he say of those, YOU ARE NOT OF MY SHEEP? Because he saw them appointed to everlasting ruin, not bought for eternal life by his blood's price. Soon after: Of those sheep neither wolf snatches, nor thief carries off, nor robber kills. He who knows what he gave for them is sure of their number. Two points follow: first, our Savior offered his blood's price for redeeming the predestined in a special way — the way from which their sure salvation follows; second, for the passed-over or non-predestined he did not offer it that way, so they are denied to have been bought for eternal life by that price — meaning an absolute, efficacious ordering to eternal life that Christ's death is to carry out and bring into act.
notes_covered: ultimum Patrum & modernorum open; Augustine In Joh. tract. 48; sheep/price; absolute efficacious ordination

title: Cap. 7 Patrum: Augustine Serm. 56 — came to redeem the predestined
latin: 2. Huic affine est illud alterum, Serm. 56. De verbis Domini, pag. 194. tom. 10. Erant praedestinati nondum congregati. Hos tamen noverat qui praedestinaverat, noverat qui redimere sanguine suo venerat. Videbat eos nondum videntes eum; noverat eos nondum credentes in eum. Quid apertius quam Christum venisse in mundum ut praedestinatos sanguine suo redimeret, atque redimeret efficaciter & infallibiliter ad participationem vitae aeternae perducendos; quo modo nunquam apud se decrevit redimere non-electos.
pass_a_gloss: 2. Kindred to this is that other place, Sermon 56 On the words of the Lord, page 194, volume 10. The predestined were not yet gathered. Yet he who had predestined them knew them; he who had come to redeem with his blood knew them. He saw them not yet seeing him; he knew them not yet believing in him. What is plainer than that Christ came into the world in order that he might redeem the predestined by his blood, and redeem them efficaciously and infallibly as ones to be led through to participation of eternal life — in which manner he never determined with himself to redeem the non-elect.
pass_b: 2. Closely related is Sermon 56 On the Lord's words (vol. 10, p. 194): The predestined were not yet gathered. Still, he who had predestined them knew them, and he who had come to redeem them with his blood knew them. He saw them while they did not yet see him; he knew them while they did not yet believe in him. Nothing is clearer: Christ came into the world to redeem the predestined by his blood — and to redeem them efficaciously and infallibly as people to be brought through to share eternal life. He never resolved with himself to redeem the non-elect in that way.
notes_covered: Augustine Serm. 56 De verbis Domini; redeem predestined; never non-elect that way

title: Cap. 7 Patrum: Augustine De natura & grat. 5 — vessels of mercy only
latin: 3. Tertium ejusdem Augustini testimonium proferemus ex libro De natura & grat. cap. 5. quod ita se habet, Qui liberantur, non vasa meritorum suorum, sed vasa misericordiae nominantur. Cujus misericordiae, nisi illius qui Christum Jesum misit in hunc mundum peccatores salvos facere? Quos praescivit, & praedestinavit, & vocavit, & justificavit, & glorificavit. Quasi dixisset, Deum ex specialis misericordiae decreto misisse Christum pro liberandis & salvandis praedestinatis efficaciter & infallibiliter; quo sensu illi soli dicuntur vasa misericordiae. Supervacaneum esset ex Augustino plura congerere, cujus sententia de absoluta praedestinatione quorundam ad vitam aeternam, deque aeterna datione eorundem Christo Mediatori, ut ab eo infallibiliter perducantur ad eandem, est omnibus in Augustino versatis notissima. Quae praedestinatio, donatio, perductio ad vitam aeternam, absque hac speciali intentione mortem ac merita sua illis applicandi, neque intelligi, neque cogitari potest. Videte caput 18. De Praed. Sanct. De bono persev. cap. 7. De cor. & grat. cap. 9.
pass_a_gloss: 3. We will bring forward a third testimony of the same Augustine from the book On nature and grace, chapter 5, which runs thus: Those who are delivered are named not vessels of their own merits, but vessels of mercy. Of whose mercy, if not of him who sent Christ Jesus into this world to save sinners? Whom he foreknew, and predestined, and called, and justified, and glorified. As if he had said that God, by a decree of special mercy, sent Christ for efficaciously and infallibly delivering and saving the predestined; in which sense they alone are called vessels of mercy. It would be superfluous to heap up more from Augustine, whose judgment concerning the absolute predestination of certain persons to eternal life, and concerning the eternal giving of the same to Christ the Mediator that by him they may be led infallibly to that life, is most well known to all who are versed in Augustine. Which predestination, giving, and leading through to eternal life cannot be understood or even thought without this special intention of applying his death and merits to them. See chapter 18 of On the Predestination of the Saints; On the gift of perseverance, chapter 7; On rebuke and grace, chapter 9.
pass_b: 3. A third witness from the same Augustine is On nature and grace, chapter 5: Those who are delivered are called not vessels of their own merits, but vessels of mercy. Whose mercy, if not his who sent Christ Jesus into this world to save sinners? Whom he foreknew, predestined, called, justified, and glorified. As if to say: by a decree of special mercy God sent Christ to deliver and save the predestined efficaciously and infallibly — and in that sense they alone are vessels of mercy. Piling up more Augustine would be wasted work. Anyone at home in him knows his teaching on the absolute predestination of some to eternal life, and on the eternal gift of those same persons to Christ the Mediator so that he may lead them to that life without fail. That predestination, gift, and leading cannot be understood — or even thought — without this special intention of applying his death and merits to them. See On the Predestination of the Saints 18; On the gift of perseverance 7; On rebuke and grace 9.
notes_covered: Augustine De natura & grat. 5; vessels of mercy; Pred. Sanct. 18 / Persev. 7 / Cor. & grat. 9

title: Cap. 7 Patrum: Ambrose — suffered for all, specially for the Church
latin: 4. Quartum testimonium ex Ambrosio peti potest, cujus haec sunt verba, Et Christus passus est pro omnibus, pro nobis tamen specialiter passus est, quia pro Ecclesia passus est. Itaque non est dubium quod plus debeat quae plus accepit, lib. 6. cap. 7. Lucae. Hic videmus ex mente Ambrosii fuisse specialem Christi patientis ad Ecclesiam suam intuitum, unde factum est ut ea ex passione Christi specialem fructum perceperit. Ita igitur Christum pro omnibus passum asserit, ut tamen voluntas & intentio Christi patientis haud omnes ex aequo respiciat, sed singulari quodam modo feratur in corpus suum mysticum, id est, primogenitorum Ecclesiam, quam sanguine suo voluit sibi acquirere, Spiritu conjungere ad infrustrabilem vitae aeternae participationem. Non passus est pro omnibus speciali hac intentione.
pass_a_gloss: 4. A fourth testimony can be sought from Ambrose, whose words are these: And Christ suffered for all, yet for us he suffered specially, because he suffered for the Church. And so there is no doubt that she owes more who has received more — book 6, chapter 7 on Luke. Here we see that, in Ambrose's mind, there was a special regard of the suffering Christ toward his Church, whence it came about that she received a special fruit from Christ's passion. He therefore affirms that Christ suffered for all in such a way that nevertheless the will and intention of the suffering Christ does not look upon all equally, but is borne in a certain singular manner upon his mystical body, that is, the Church of the firstborn, which by his blood he willed to acquire for himself, and by the Spirit to join to an unfrustrating participation of eternal life. He did not suffer for all with this special intention.
pass_b: 4. Ambrose supplies a fourth witness: And Christ suffered for all, yet for us he suffered specially, because he suffered for the Church. So she who received more doubtless owes more (On Luke, book 6, chapter 7). On Ambrose's reading, the suffering Christ had a special regard for his Church, and from that she drew a special fruit of the passion. He can say Christ suffered for all, and still hold that the will and intention of the suffering Christ does not regard everyone alike, but turns in a singular way upon his mystical body — the Church of the firstborn — which he meant by his blood to make his own and by the Spirit to join to a share in eternal life that cannot fail. He did not suffer for all under that special intention.
notes_covered: Ambrose On Luke 6.7; suffered for all / specially for Church; mystical body

title: Cap. 7 Patrum: Remigius — Son delivered for predestined elect alone
latin: 5. Ambrosium sequatur Remigius Episcopus Rhemensis, qui haec scribit, in Rom. viii. Quos praedestinavit sive praefinivit secum regnaturos in aeterna beatitudine, hos vocavit, hos & justificavit per passionem suam, per baptismum & fidem exornatam bonis operibus, & justificavit usque ad finem seculi. Paulo post, in haec verba, Qui proprio Filio non pepercit, id est, inquit Remigius, a morte non servavit, sed pro nobis omnibus praedestinatis ad vitam aeternam illum tradidit. Quae omnia demonstrant Christum pro electis, & solis electis, cum proposito certo eosdem salvandi passum: quae est ipsissima specialis intentio, quam nos stabilire conamur, quamque ad solos electos restringendam tuemur, in hac Christi oblatione.
pass_a_gloss: 5. Let Remigius, Bishop of Rheims, follow Ambrose, who writes thus on Romans 8: Those whom he predestined or predetermined to reign with him in eternal blessedness, these he called, these also he justified through his passion, through baptism and faith adorned with good works, and he justified them unto the end of the age. A little later, on these words, Who spared not his own Son — that is, says Remigius, he did not keep him from death, but for all of us predestined to eternal life he delivered him. All which things demonstrate that Christ suffered for the elect, and for the elect alone, with a sure purpose of saving them: which is the very special intention that we are trying to establish, and that we maintain must be restricted to the elect alone, in this offering of Christ.
pass_b: 5. After Ambrose comes Remigius of Rheims on Romans 8: Those he predestined — or marked out beforehand — to reign with him in eternal blessedness he also called and justified through his passion, through baptism and faith adorned with good works, and he justified them to the world's end. Soon after, on Who did not spare his own Son, Remigius says: he did not keep him from death, but delivered him for all of us predestined to eternal life. That shows Christ suffered for the elect, and for them alone, with a fixed purpose to save them — the very special intention we are establishing, and which we insist must be limited to the elect alone in this offering of Christ.
notes_covered: Remigius Rhemensis on Rom 8; Son delivered for predestined; elect-only special intent

title: Cap. 7 Patrum: Fulgentius — special will and predestination in Christ
latin: 6. Fulgentius, De Incarn. & grat. Jesu Chr. cap. 29. p. 92. Biblioth. Patr. tom. 6. Hi qui voluntatem Dei, qua omnes homines vult salvos fieri, aequalem circa redimendos & damnandos existimant, cum interrogati fuerint cur Deus velit omnes homines salvos fieri, nec tamen omnes salvi fiant, quid respondebunt? Innuit doctissimus Fulgentius, Deum speciali voluntate illorum salutem per Christum procurandam decrevisse qui de facto salvantur; eosque qui contrarium affirmant, nihil solidi habere quod respondeant, quando urgentur ut ostendant, unde hoc discrimen oriatur, quod quidam morte Christi reapse salvantur, alii non salvantur. Ad humanarum voluntatum discrimen hoc revocari non posse demonstrat. cap. 30. & 31. 7. Adjungo aliud testimonium ejusdem Fulgentii, lib. 3. De verit. Praedest. Quos Deus praedestinavit in adoptionem Filiorum, hos non solum ad praemium glorificationis sed ad gratiam justificationis ante mundi constitutionem in Christo praedestinatos, & hujus praedestinationis beneficio secundum propositum vocatos & justificatos, nullus debet ambigere Christianus. Qui non ambigit electos Dei filios fuisse in Christo tam ad gratiam, quam ad gloriam ante mundi constitutionem praedestinatos, ille ultro fatebitur, mortem meritumque Christi fuisse speciali quadam ratione pro eisdem electis ordinatum & acceptatum, ut inde possent hanc gratiam & gloriam sibi destinatam infallibiliter obtinere.
pass_a_gloss: 6. Fulgentius, On the Incarnation and grace of Jesus Christ, chapter 29, page 92, Library of the Fathers, volume 6. Those who think the will of God by which he wills all human beings to be saved is equal concerning the redeemed and the damned — when they have been asked why God wills all human beings to be saved and yet not all are saved — what will they answer? The most learned Fulgentius hints that God by a special will decreed that the salvation of those who are in fact saved should be procured through Christ; and that those who affirm the contrary have nothing solid to answer when they are pressed to show whence this difference arises, that some are actually saved by Christ's death and others are not saved. He demonstrates that this cannot be referred to a difference of human wills — chapters 30 and 31. 7. I add another testimony of the same Fulgentius, book 3 On the truth of Predestination. Those whom God predestined to the adoption of sons — that no Christian ought to doubt they were predestined in Christ before the foundation of the world not only to the reward of glorification but to the grace of justification, and by the benefit of this predestination called and justified according to purpose. Whoever does not doubt that the elect sons of God were predestined in Christ both to grace and to glory before the world's foundation will freely confess that Christ's death and merit were ordained and accepted in a certain special manner for those same elect, so that from thence they might infallibly obtain this grace and glory destined for them.
pass_b: 6. Fulgentius, On the Incarnation and grace of Jesus Christ 29 (Bibliotheca Patrum, vol. 6, p. 92): Those who treat God's will that all be saved as the same toward the redeemed and the damned — when asked why God wills all to be saved and yet not all are — what answer have they? Fulgentius implies that God by a special will decreed to procure, through Christ, the salvation of those who are in fact saved; and that their opponents have nothing solid left when pressed to explain why some are actually saved by Christ's death and others are not. He shows this difference cannot be reduced to a difference of human wills (chs. 30-31). 7. Another from the same Fulgentius, On the truth of Predestination, book 3: No Christian should doubt that those God predestined to the adoption of sons were predestined in Christ before the world's foundation not only to the reward of glory but to the grace of justification, and by that predestination's benefit called and justified according to purpose. Anyone who grants that God's elect sons were so predestined in Christ to grace and glory will freely admit that Christ's death and merit were ordained and accepted in a special way for those same elect, so that from them they might obtain without fail the grace and glory marked out for them.
notes_covered: Fulgentius Incarn. & grat. 29-31; De verit. Praed. 3; special will; elect predestined in Christ

title: Cap. 7 Patrum close: Paschasius, Gregory, Bernard before Scholastics
latin: 8. Paschasius, Biblioth. Patr. tom. 9. pag. 930. in illa verba Matth. i. 21. Saluum faciet populum suum a peccatis, sic scribit, Hinc Zacharias inquit, Et fecit REDEMPTIONEM PLEBIS SUAE IN DOMO DAVID PUERI SUI. Ergo quam sua praescivit, illam proculdubio venit salvare; reliquos omnes occulto suo judicio in massa damnationis reliquit. Quibus verbis docet Christum venisse in mundum, ac mortem subiisse, speciali quadam intentione salvandi praedestinatos, quam specialem intentionem de aliorum salute efficienda minime habuit, utcunque omnibus sub conditione Fidei salutem parabilem reddere voluerit. 9. Gregorius Magnus, moral. lib. 22. cap. 18. pag. 132. Unigenito Dei Filio pro homine interpellare, est apud coaeternum Patrem seipsum hominem demonstrare: eique pro humana natura rogasse, est eandem naturam in Divinitatis suae celsitudine suscepisse. Interpellat igitur pro nobis non voce, sed miseratione, quia quod damnari in electis noluit, suscipiendo liberavit. Notanda sunt imprimis illa ultima verba, quibus clare indicatur, Christum in toto suo officio Mediatorio specialem intuitum habuisse ad electos infallibiliter liberandos. 10. Bernardus in Psalmum, Qui habitat in adjutorio Altissimi, vers. 9. Christus, inquit, pro amicis mortuus est, hoc est acquirendis, videlicet ut amicos faceret ex inimicis. Paulo post, Sic ergo Christus secundum tempus pro impiis mortuus est, secundum praedestinationem autem pro fratribus & amicis. Quod perinde est ac si dixisset, Christum morientem in cruce ad praedestinatos suos fratres & futuros amicos singularem respectum habuisse.
pass_a_gloss: 8. Paschasius, Library of the Fathers, volume 9, page 930, on those words of Matthew 1:21, He shall save his people from sins, writes thus: Hence Zechariah says, And he has made REDEMPTION OF HIS PEOPLE IN THE HOUSE OF DAVID HIS SERVANT. Therefore the people whom he foreknew as his own he doubtless came to save; all the rest he left by his hidden judgment in the mass of damnation. By which words he teaches that Christ came into the world and underwent death with a certain special intention of saving the predestined — which special intention of effecting the salvation of others he by no means had, however much he willed to make salvation obtainable for all under the condition of Faith. 9. Gregory the Great, Morals, book 22, chapter 18, page 132. For the Only-begotten Son of God to intercede for man is to show himself as man before the coeternal Father; and to have asked for him on behalf of human nature is to have taken up that same nature into the height of his Divinity. He therefore intercedes for us not by voice but by compassion, because what he did not will to be damned in the elect he liberated by taking it up. Those last words especially are to be noted, by which it is clearly indicated that Christ in his whole Mediator's office had a special regard toward infallibly freeing the elect. 10. Bernard on the Psalm He who dwells in the help of the Most High, verse 9. Christ, he says, died for friends — that is, for those to be acquired, namely that he might make friends out of enemies. A little later: So then Christ according to time died for the ungodly, but according to predestination for brothers and friends. Which is as if he had said that Christ dying on the cross had a singular respect toward his predestined brothers and future friends.
pass_b: 8. Paschasius (Bibliotheca Patrum, vol. 9, p. 930) on Matthew 1:21, He shall save his people from their sins: Hence Zechariah says, And he made REDEMPTION OF HIS PEOPLE IN THE HOUSE OF DAVID HIS SERVANT. So the people he foreknew as his he surely came to save; all the rest he left, by his hidden judgment, in the mass of damnation. That teaches Christ came and died with a special intention to save the predestined — an intention he did not have for making others' salvation actual, even while he willed to make salvation obtainable for all under the condition of faith. 9. Gregory the Great, Morals 22.18 (p. 132): For the Only-begotten to intercede for man is to present himself as man before the coeternal Father; to ask for human nature is to have taken that nature up into his Divinity's height. So he intercedes for us not by voice but by compassion, because what he would not have damned in the elect he set free by taking it up. Those last words show plainly that in his whole Mediator's work Christ kept a special eye on freeing the elect without fail. 10. Bernard on Psalm He who dwells in the help of the Most High, verse 9: Christ died for friends — that is, for friends to be won, to make friends out of enemies. A little later: So according to time Christ died for the ungodly, but according to predestination for brothers and friends — as much as to say that Christ dying on the cross had a singular regard for his predestined brothers and future friends.
notes_covered: Paschasius Matth 1:21; Gregory Morals 22.18; Bernard Qui habitat; before Sed missis Scholastics
